VIDEO.title: This SECRET Is HIDDEN in Matthew 6! (Matthew 6:1-18)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: The Father is unseen, so His children give, pray and fast unseen.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 6:1-18: don't do your righteousness to be seen. Three examples follow: giving to the poor, prayer (with the Lord's Prayer) and fasting. Each time, the hypocrites 'have their reward in full,' and 'your Father who sees what is done in secret will reward you.'

First, a promise behind the whole sermon: God must change the heart. Jeremiah 31:33 (the law written on the heart) and Ezekiel 36:25-27 (clean water, a new heart, God's Spirit), which Jesus draws on with Nicodemus in John 3. The sermon is not 'just try harder.'
A hypocrite in Jesus' day was a Greek stage actor. Jesus' disciples must not perform their righteousness for applause.

The teacher suggests the whole sermon may be a chiasm with the Lord's Prayer at its center, and the prayer itself a chiasm centered on 'on earth as it is in heaven.' He says plainly this is debated and he is still chewing on it.
The key word is 'reward.' It starts at 5:46 ('what reward do you have?'), so chapter 6 extends the end of chapter 5: string together 5:20, 5:46, 5:48 and 6:1 and it's all connected.

The lesson: the Father blesses everyone, the just and the unjust, not to be seen but because He loves. So we do our righteousness in secret, because our Father is in secret. The commands reveal the Father's heart, and knowing Him leads to intimacy with Him.
QUOTES: Something must take place in our hearts, and it has to be done by God.
A hypocrite in Jesus' day was a Greek actor... all of this was just a performance, and it was meant for the crowd's applause.
Our heavenly Father is in secret. Our actions and our motives should be hidden, just like our Father.
The commands of Jesus actually reveal the Father.
Deeper understanding of the Father can lead to deeper intimacy with the Father.

method.h: Lay chapters 5 and 6 side by side
method.p: The teacher asks you to open Matthew 5 on the left and Matthew 6 on the right, and to track one repeated word: 'reward.' Underline it every time (5:46; 6:1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 16, 18). Then look for other repeated words and phrases on your own.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Beware of doing your righteousness before men to be noticed by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.
But you, when you pray, go into your inner room, and when you have shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret, and your Father who sees what is done in secret will reward you.
Your kingdom come. / Your will be done, / On earth as it is in heaven.

HEART.title: The law written on the heart

src.text: But this is the covenant which I will cut with the house of Israel after those days,” declares Yahweh: “I will put My law within them, and on their heart I will write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be My people.

lines.text: Something ontologically significant must take place, done by God to our hearts. The Sermon on the Mount presupposes these promises.
Hebrews quotes this passage at length as fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 8:8-12), and Jesus speaks of 'the new covenant in My blood' (Luke 22:20).

HEART.title: Clean water, a new heart, My Spirit

src.text: Moreover, I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes, and you will be careful to do My judgments.

lines.text: This is what Jesus refers to when He tells Nicodemus about being born of water and the Spirit (John 3): the cleansing water of Ezekiel 36:25 and the Spirit of 36:26-27.
Jesus chides Nicodemus as 'the teacher of Israel' for not understanding (John 3:10), which fits an Old Testament background like Ezekiel 36.

src.text: but whoever keeps His word, truly in him the love of God has been perfected. By this we know that we are in Him: the one who says he abides in Him ought himself to walk in the same manner as He walked.

lines.text: The sermon should not freak a disciple out with 'a ton of new commands.' It connects to the psalmist's love of God's law (Psalm 119), to abiding in Jesus (John 15:1-11) and to 1 John 2: we perform our righteousness in the same way He did.

THREE.title: When you give to the poor

left.text: Therefore, when you give to the poor, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be glorified by men.

right.text: But when you give to the poor, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving will be in secret; and your Father who sees what is done in secret will reward you.

lines.text: The 'greater' righteousness of 5:20 is not more actions performed for others to see. It is righteousness that pierces and transforms the heart, unseen by the person on the street.

Whether 'sound a trumpet' is a figure of speech or points to something real is debated. The Mishnah describes thirteen 'collection horns' in the temple, 'narrow at the top and wide at the bottom' (Shekalim 6:1, William Davidson edition, CC BY-NC, via Sefaria).

THREE.note: Augustine on the left hand: 'the left hand seems to have no more suitable meaning than just this delight in praise' (On the Sermon on the Mount, Book 2).

left.text: And when you pray, you are not to be like the hypocrites; for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and on the street corners so that they may be seen by men.

right.text: But you, when you pray, go into your inner room, and when you have shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret, and your Father who sees what is done in secret will reward you.

lines.text: Not like the Greek actors who blow the trumpets, not like those who do things to be lauded on the street corners, but like the Father does.

A second warning follows: 'do not use meaningless repetition as the Gentiles do... for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him' (6:7-8). The 'inner room' (tameion) was often a storeroom, the one room with a door.

THREE.title: When you fast

left.text: Now whenever you fast, do not put on a gloomy face as the hypocrites do, for they neglect their appearance so that they will be noticed by men when they are fasting.

right.text: But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face so that your fasting will not be noticed by men, but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees what is done in secret will reward you.

lines.text: Once again Jesus contrasts His disciples with the Greek actors, the hypocrites who perform for applause.

There is a wordplay in 6:16: they make their faces disappear (aphanizō, 'neglect their appearance') so that they may appear (phainō, 'be noticed'). Isaiah had already asked what kind of fast God chooses (Isaiah 58:5-7).

THREE.note: The Didache, an early Christian manual, says: 'But let not your fasts be with the hypocrites; for they fast on the second and fifth day of the week; but fast on the fourth day and the Preparation (Friday).'

left.text: I will prove the holiness of My great name which has been profaned among the nations

right.text: Our Father who is in heaven, / Hallowed be Your name.

lines.text: The same chapter of Ezekiel that promises a new heart begins with God making His name holy. To pray 'hallowed be Your name' is to ask God to do it.

PETITIONS.title: On earth as it is in heaven

left.text: And God created man in His own image, in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.

right.text: Your kingdom come. / Your will be done, / On earth as it is in heaven.

lines.text: If the prayer is a chiasm, this line is its center, and it would make sense of the sermon's focus on the kingdom. It takes us back to Genesis 1, being created in the image of God to mirror God.
The teacher says this layout is debated, and he is still chewing on it. Many read the prayer simply as two sets of requests: three for God's name, kingdom and will, then requests for our needs.

left.text: Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day

right.text: Give us this day our daily bread.

lines.text: Bread for each day, gathered day by day: Israel learned daily dependence in the wilderness. The rare word for 'daily' (epiousios) is discussed below in Hebrew and Greek words.

PETITIONS.title: Forgive us, as we forgive

src.text: For if you forgive others for their transgressions, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive others, then your Father will not forgive your transgressions.

lines.text: The only petition Jesus explains afterward. He tells a whole parable about it later, ending: 'My heavenly Father will also do the same to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts' (Matthew 18:35). 'Do not lead us into temptation' recalls Jesus' own testing (4:1) and Gethsemane (26:41).

PETITIONS.note: Cyprian of Carthage (c. AD 252): 'Our prayer is public and common; and when we pray, we pray not for one, but for the whole people, because we the whole people are one' (On the Lord's Prayer, 8).

PEOPLE.name: Jesus
PEOPLE.video: Reveals the Father: every 'do this' shows how the Father operates, unseen, blessing all.
PEOPLE.bg: Jesus Himself often prayed alone: 'He went up on the mountain by Himself to pray' (Matthew 14:23).

PEOPLE.name: The Father in heaven
PEOPLE.video: Unseen, in secret, blessing the just and the unjust because He loves, not to be seen.
PEOPLE.bg: 'Father' appears ten times in 6:1-18 in the LSB, more than anywhere else in the sermon.

PEOPLE.name: The hypocrites
PEOPLE.video: The Greek word for a stage actor: people who perform righteousness for applause. In the sermon they are the scribes and Pharisees of 5:20.
PEOPLE.bg: Matthew uses 'hypocrites' more than any other Gospel, especially in the woes of chapter 23.

PEOPLE.name: The Gentiles
PEOPLE.video: Their prayers heap up many words, as if to be heard for them (6:7).
PEOPLE.bg: The pagan prayers of the day often piled up divine names and titles to make sure the right god was addressed.

PEOPLE.name: Nicodemus
PEOPLE.video: Jesus tells him about being born of water and the Spirit (John 3), pointing back to Ezekiel 36.
PEOPLE.bg: A Pharisee and 'a ruler of the Jews' who came to Jesus by night (John 3:1-2) and later helped bury Him (John 19:39).

PEOPLE.name: The disciples and the crowds
PEOPLE.video: The audience again: the disciples, with the crowds who came and sat to hear.
PEOPLE.bg: The Lord's Prayer is given to disciples: 'Pray, then, in this way' (6:9). Luke places it after a disciple asks, 'Lord, teach us to pray' (Luke 11:1).

PLACES.name: Capernaum
PLACES.note: Jesus' home base. The white synagogue visitors see is later, built on an older basalt foundation.

PLACES.name: Magdala
PLACES.note: A 1st-century synagogue, in use in Jesus' day, was uncovered here in 2009.

PLACES.name: Chorazin
PLACES.note: Its basalt synagogue ruins date from a few centuries after Jesus.

PLACES.name: Arbel
PLACES.note: Cliffs above the lake with the remains of a later synagogue.

PLACES.name: Mount of Beatitudes
PLACES.note: The traditional site of the sermon.

PLACES.name: Tiberias
PLACES.note: Herod Antipas' capital, founded around AD 20.

PLACES.name: Bethsaida
PLACES.note: Home town of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44).

PLACES.name: Nazareth
PLACES.note: Jesus' hometown, where He taught in the synagogue (Luke 4:16).

TERMS.def: Greek hypokritēs: a stage actor, who played a part behind a mask. Jesus uses it for people whose religion is a performance.
Here, acts of devotion: giving, prayer and fasting, the three pillars of Jewish piety.
Greek eleēmosynē, from eleos, mercy: the root of 'alms.' Linked to 'Blessed are the merciful' (5:7).
Apechō was used on business receipts: 'paid in full.' The applause is all they will get.
A mirrored pattern with a center. The video suggests the whole sermon and the Lord's Prayer may each be chiastic, and says this is debated.
The model prayer of 6:9-13 (also Luke 11:2-4). The closing doxology, 'For Yours is the kingdom...,' is in brackets in the LSB because the earliest manuscripts lack it.
Going without food for a time to seek God. The Day of Atonement's 'humble your souls' (Leviticus 16:29) was kept by fasting; the Pharisee in Jesus' parable says, 'I fast twice a week' (Luke 18:12).
God's promise to write His law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31-34), the backdrop the video gives for the sermon.

WORDS.gloss: Wages, pay, reward. The noun in 5:46 and 6:1, 2, 5, 16.
To give back, repay (LSB 'reward'). The Father's answer in 6:4, 6, 18.
To receive in full; a word used on receipts. Look up: BDAG, ἀπέχω.
Actor, pretender: one who plays a part.
To look at, behold, as a spectator (LSB 'noticed'). Related to theatron, 'theater.'
Hidden, secret ('crypt'). 6:18 uses the related kryphaios (G2931a).
To babble, use empty words (LSB 'use meaningless repetition'). Found only here in the New Testament.
To make holy, treat as holy (LSB 'Hallowed').
Daily: a rare word whose exact sense is debated ('for today,' 'for tomorrow,' or 'needed'). Look up: BDAG, ἐπιούσιος.
Debt; sin pictured as a debt owed to God. 6:14-15 switches to paraptōma, 'transgression.'
Testing, temptation: the same root as Jesus' testing in the wilderness (4:1).
To make unseen, disfigure (LSB 'neglect their appearance'); a play on phainō, 'appear.'
Heart: the inner person, mind and will. 'On their heart I will write it.'

BACKGROUND.p: Giving to the poor, prayer and fasting were the core acts of Jewish devotion. Jesus assumes His disciples will do all three: 'when you give,' 'when you pray,' 'when you fast.'
Theaters stood in the Decapolis cities and later in Sepphoris, near Nazareth, so 'hypocrite' was a familiar word. Actors wore masks to play their parts.
Jews prayed at fixed times, often morning, afternoon and evening, wherever they were (compare Daniel 6:10; Acts 3:1). Being 'caught' on a street corner at prayer time could become a show.

The Pharisee in Jesus' parable fasts 'twice a week' (Luke 18:12); the Didache names Monday and Thursday as the 'hypocrites'' days. Fasters might skip washing and oiling their hair and wear sackcloth and ashes. Jesus says: look normal.

BACKGROUND.h: The Lord's Prayer in the early church
BACKGROUND.p: The Didache, an early Christian manual (c. AD 100), gives the prayer in Matthew's form with a doxology and says: 'Thrice in the day thus pray.'

WITNESSES.text: Neither pray as the hypocrites; but as the Lord commanded in His Gospel, thus pray: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be Your name.
WITNESSES.src: Didache 8 (Roberts-Donaldson translation, public domain). It closes: 'Thrice in the day thus pray.'

WITNESSES.text: And well has He called them hypocrites for the mask was of mercy, but the spirit of cruelty and inhumanity.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 19, on 6:2. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: Our prayer is public and common; and when we pray, we pray not for one, but for the whole people, because we the whole people are one.
WITNESSES.src: On the Lord's Prayer, 8. Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5 (public domain).

DEBATES.h: Is the whole sermon a chiasm?
DEBATES.p: Some scholars arrange Matthew 5-7 symmetrically with the Lord's Prayer at the center; others see a different structure (for example, 'the Law and the Prophets' at 5:17 and 7:12 framing the body). The video offers it as an invitation to study.

DEBATES.h: Is the Lord's Prayer a chiasm?
DEBATES.p: The video's center is 'on earth as it is in heaven.' Many read the prayer as three 'Your' petitions followed by three or four 'us' petitions. Either way, heaven's will on earth is a key line.

The video stresses actors performing for applause. Others stress that Jesus' 'hypocrites' are also self-deceived: they 'say things and do not do them' (23:3). Both point to a gap between show and heart.
Epiousios is almost unknown outside the Lord's Prayer: bread for today, for the coming day, or what is needed. Some early writers also read it of spiritual bread.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The captions say 'Matthew chapter 6 verses 1-8'; the passage read is 6:1-18.
In English 'reward' repeats through 6:1-18, but Greek uses two words: the noun misthos (5:46; 6:1, 2, 5, 16) and the verb apodidōmi, 'repay' (6:4, 6, 18). The chain the video traces still holds.
Hypokritēs did mean a stage actor. The touring troupes with trumpets and painted faces are an illustration rather than something the text says; Greek actors usually wore masks.
'Everything Jesus says in the Gospels is either a quotation from the Old Testament or an allusion to it' is a strong claim. Very much of it is, which is why the video's method works so well.
The two chiasms (the whole sermon and the Lord's Prayer) are proposals; the video says so itself.

QUESTIONS: The video's side study: list every word or phrase Jesus repeats in 6:1-18. What patterns do you see?
Why does the sermon need Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 behind it? What happens if we read it as 'just try harder'?
Which of the three (giving, prayer, fasting) do you find hardest to do 'in secret'? Why?
Pray the Lord's Prayer slowly. Which line stands out to you as the center this week?
The video says the commands reveal the Father. What does 6:1-18 show you about the Father's heart?
What is the lesson for you today?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience: our heavenly Father extends His blessings to all, the just and the unjust, not to be seen but because He loves. So we perform our righteousness the same way, in secret, because our Father is in secret. Disciples must not act like actors blowing trumpets, but like the Father. The commands reveal His heart, His desires and His motives, and deeper understanding of the Father can lead to deeper intimacy with the Father. Now it's your turn: what is the lesson for you today?
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): try one secret act this week from each of the three: give something no one will know about, pray once behind a shut door, and skip one meal to pray without telling anyone. Then ask the Father what He showed you.

# Matthew 6:1-18 Study Notes: This SECRET Is HIDDEN in Matthew 6! (Matthew 6:1-18)
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T4CrkP8KMu4
Channel: Every Word | Length: 25:05 | Series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)
Series hub: https://shea-nelson.github.io/workout-app/bible/
Study page: https://shea-nelson.github.io/workout-app/bible/matthew-8/
PDF for Goodnotes: https://shea-nelson.github.io/workout-app/bible/assets/Matthew-Ep08-Your-Father-Who-Sees-in-Secret.pdf
Translation: Legacy Standard Bible (LSB). The video reads from another English translation; quotations here are LSB. Notes marked [Background] are added study helps, not from the video.

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 6:1-18: don't do your righteousness to be seen. Three examples follow: giving to the poor, prayer (with the Lord's Prayer) and fasting. Each time, the hypocrites 'have their reward in full,' and 'your Father who sees what is done in secret will reward you.'
- First, a promise behind the whole sermon: God must change the heart. Jeremiah 31:33 (the law written on the heart) and Ezekiel 36:25-27 (clean water, a new heart, God's Spirit), which Jesus draws on with Nicodemus in John 3. The sermon is not 'just try harder.'
- A hypocrite in Jesus' day was a Greek stage actor. Jesus' disciples must not perform their righteousness for applause.
- The teacher suggests the whole sermon may be a chiasm with the Lord's Prayer at its center, and the prayer itself a chiasm centered on 'on earth as it is in heaven.' He says plainly this is debated and he is still chewing on it.
- The key word is 'reward.' It starts at 5:46 ('what reward do you have?'), so chapter 6 extends the end of chapter 5: string together 5:20, 5:46, 5:48 and 6:1 and it's all connected.
- The lesson: the Father blesses everyone, the just and the unjust, not to be seen but because He loves. So we do our righteousness in secret, because our Father is in secret. The commands reveal the Father's heart, and knowing Him leads to intimacy with Him.

## Key quotes from the video (auto-captions, lightly cleaned)
> "Something must take place in our hearts, and it has to be done by God."
> "A hypocrite in Jesus' day was a Greek actor... all of this was just a performance, and it was meant for the crowd's applause."
> "Our heavenly Father is in secret. Our actions and our motives should be hidden, just like our Father."
> "The commands of Jesus actually reveal the Father."
> "Deeper understanding of the Father can lead to deeper intimacy with the Father."

### Lay chapters 5 and 6 side by side
The teacher asks you to open Matthew 5 on the left and Matthew 6 on the right, and to track one repeated word: 'reward.' Underline it every time (5:46; 6:1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 16, 18). Then look for other repeated words and phrases on your own.

## First, a new heart
1. Promise · Jeremiah 31: The law written on the heart
   New covenant Jeremiah 31:33: "But this is the covenant which I will cut with the house of Israel after those days,” declares Yahweh: “I will put My law within them, and on their heart I will write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be My people." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Jeremiah+31:33
   (video) Something ontologically significant must take place, done by God to our hearts. The Sermon on the Mount presupposes these promises.
   [Background] Hebrews quotes this passage at length as fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 8:8-12), and Jesus speaks of 'the new covenant in My blood' (Luke 22:20). (Hebrews 8:8-12; Luke 22:20)
2. Promise · Ezekiel 36: Clean water, a new heart, My Spirit
   New heart Ezekiel 36:26-27: "Moreover, I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes, and you will be careful to do My judgments." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Ezekiel+36:26-27
   (video) This is what Jesus refers to when He tells Nicodemus about being born of water and the Spirit (John 3): the cleansing water of Ezekiel 36:25 and the Spirit of 36:26-27. (Ezekiel 36:25; John 3:5)
   [Background] Jesus chides Nicodemus as 'the teacher of Israel' for not understanding (John 3:10), which fits an Old Testament background like Ezekiel 36. (John 3:10)
3. The result · 1 John 2: Walk as He walked
   Abide 1 John 2:5-6: "but whoever keeps His word, truly in him the love of God has been perfected. By this we know that we are in Him: the one who says he abides in Him ought himself to walk in the same manner as He walked." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=1+John+2:5-6
   (video) The sermon should not freak a disciple out with 'a ton of new commands.' It connects to the psalmist's love of God's law (Psalm 119), to abiding in Jesus (John 15:1-11) and to 1 John 2: we perform our righteousness in the same way He did. (Psalm 119:11; John 15:9-11)

## String the verses together
Matthew 5:20, 46, 48 and 6:1 (LSB)
Matthew 5:20 For I say to you that unless your righteousness surpasses that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.
Matthew 5:46 For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?
Matthew 5:48 Therefore you are to be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
Matthew 6:1 Beware of doing your righteousness before men to be noticed by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.
'It's all connected. You see it?' The righteousness that surpasses (5:20) is love like the Father's (5:46-48), done for the Father, not for an audience (6:1).

## Giving, prayer and fasting, in secret
The reward chain (LSB)
Starts here Matthew 5:46 For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have?
Warning Matthew 6:1 Beware of doing your righteousness before men to be noticed by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.
    Giving Matthew 6:2 Truly I say to you, they have their reward in full.
        Giving Matthew 6:4 so that your giving will be in secret; and your Father who sees what is done in secret will reward you.
    Prayer Matthew 6:5 Truly I say to you, they have their reward in full.
        Prayer Matthew 6:6 pray to your Father who is in secret, and your Father who sees what is done in secret will reward you.
    Fasting Matthew 6:16 Truly I say to you, they have their reward in full.
        Fasting Matthew 6:18 so that your fasting will not be noticed by men, but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees what is done in secret will reward you.
Coral: the hypocrites are paid in full by applause. Teal: the Father who sees in secret rewards.
1. Giving · Matthew 6:2-4: When you give to the poor
   Like the hypocrites (Matthew 6:2, LSB): "Therefore, when you give to the poor, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be glorified by men."
   Like your Father (Matthew 6:3-4, LSB): "But when you give to the poor, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving will be in secret; and your Father who sees what is done in secret will reward you."
   (video) The 'greater' righteousness of 5:20 is not more actions performed for others to see. It is righteousness that pierces and transforms the heart, unseen by the person on the street.
   [Background] Whether 'sound a trumpet' is a figure of speech or points to something real is debated. The Mishnah describes thirteen 'collection horns' in the temple, 'narrow at the top and wide at the bottom' (Shekalim 6:1, William Davidson edition, CC BY-NC, via Sefaria).
   Augustine on the left hand: 'the left hand seems to have no more suitable meaning than just this delight in praise' (On the Sermon on the Mount, Book 2).
2. Prayer · Matthew 6:5-8: When you pray
   Like the hypocrites (Matthew 6:5, LSB): "And when you pray, you are not to be like the hypocrites; for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and on the street corners so that they may be seen by men."
   Like your Father (Matthew 6:6, LSB): "But you, when you pray, go into your inner room, and when you have shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret, and your Father who sees what is done in secret will reward you."
   (video) Not like the Greek actors who blow the trumpets, not like those who do things to be lauded on the street corners, but like the Father does.
   [Background] A second warning follows: 'do not use meaningless repetition as the Gentiles do... for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him' (6:7-8). The 'inner room' (tameion) was often a storeroom, the one room with a door. (Matthew 6:7-8; 2 Kings 4:33)
3. Fasting · Matthew 6:16-18: When you fast
   Like the hypocrites (Matthew 6:16, LSB): "Now whenever you fast, do not put on a gloomy face as the hypocrites do, for they neglect their appearance so that they will be noticed by men when they are fasting."
   Like your Father (Matthew 6:17-18, LSB): "But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face so that your fasting will not be noticed by men, but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees what is done in secret will reward you."
   (video) Once again Jesus contrasts His disciples with the Greek actors, the hypocrites who perform for applause.
   [Background] There is a wordplay in 6:16: they make their faces disappear (aphanizō, 'neglect their appearance') so that they may appear (phainō, 'be noticed'). Isaiah had already asked what kind of fast God chooses (Isaiah 58:5-7). (Isaiah 58:3-7)
   The Didache, an early Christian manual, says: 'But let not your fasts be with the hypocrites; for they fast on the second and fifth day of the week; but fast on the fourth day and the Preparation (Friday).'

## The Lord's Prayer
Matthew 6:9-13 (LSB), in the video's suggested shape
Matthew 6:9 Our Father who is in heaven,
    Matthew 6:9 Hallowed be Your name.
        Matthew 6:10 Your kingdom come.
            Matthew 6:10 Your will be done,
                Matthew 6:10 On earth as it is in heaven.   <- the video's suggested center (debated)
            Matthew 6:11 Give us this day our daily bread.
        Matthew 6:12 And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
    Matthew 6:13 And do not lead us into temptation,
Matthew 6:13 but deliver us from the evil one.
One proposed layout, not the only one. The LSB adds in brackets 'For Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen,' which the earliest manuscripts do not have.
1. Matthew 6:9: Hallowed be Your name
   Ezekiel (Ezekiel 36:23, LSB): "I will prove the holiness of My great name which has been profaned among the nations"
   Jesus (Matthew 6:9, LSB): "Our Father who is in heaven, / Hallowed be Your name."
   [Background] The same chapter of Ezekiel that promises a new heart begins with God making His name holy. To pray 'hallowed be Your name' is to ask God to do it. (Ezekiel 36:22-23)
2. Matthew 6:10 · The video's center: On earth as it is in heaven
   Creation (Genesis 1:27, LSB): "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them."
   Jesus (Matthew 6:10, LSB): "Your kingdom come. / Your will be done, / On earth as it is in heaven."
   (video) If the prayer is a chiasm, this line is its center, and it would make sense of the sermon's focus on the kingdom. It takes us back to Genesis 1, being created in the image of God to mirror God.
   [Debated] The teacher says this layout is debated, and he is still chewing on it. Many read the prayer simply as two sets of requests: three for God's name, kingdom and will, then requests for our needs.
3. Matthew 6:11: Our daily bread
   The manna (Exodus 16:4, LSB): "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day"
   Jesus (Matthew 6:11, LSB): "Give us this day our daily bread."
   [Background] Bread for each day, gathered day by day: Israel learned daily dependence in the wilderness. The rare word for 'daily' (epiousios) is discussed below in Hebrew and Greek words. (Exodus 16:4-5; Deuteronomy 8:3)
4. Matthew 6:12-15: Forgive us, as we forgive
   Repeated Matthew 6:14-15: "For if you forgive others for their transgressions, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive others, then your Father will not forgive your transgressions." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+6:14-15
   [Background] The only petition Jesus explains afterward. He tells a whole parable about it later, ending: 'My heavenly Father will also do the same to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts' (Matthew 18:35). 'Do not lead us into temptation' recalls Jesus' own testing (4:1) and Gethsemane (26:41). (Matthew 18:21-35; Matthew 26:41)
   Cyprian of Carthage (c. AD 252): 'Our prayer is public and common; and when we pray, we pray not for one, but for the whole people, because we the whole people are one' (On the Lord's Prayer, 8).

## Key people
- Jesus: Reveals the Father: every 'do this' shows how the Father operates, unseen, blessing all. [Background] Jesus Himself often prayed alone: 'He went up on the mountain by Himself to pray' (Matthew 14:23).
- The Father in heaven: Unseen, in secret, blessing the just and the unjust because He loves, not to be seen. [Background] 'Father' appears ten times in 6:1-18 in the LSB, more than anywhere else in the sermon.
- The hypocrites: The Greek word for a stage actor: people who perform righteousness for applause. In the sermon they are the scribes and Pharisees of 5:20. [Background] Matthew uses 'hypocrites' more than any other Gospel, especially in the woes of chapter 23.
- The Gentiles: Their prayers heap up many words, as if to be heard for them (6:7). [Background] The pagan prayers of the day often piled up divine names and titles to make sure the right god was addressed.
- Nicodemus: Jesus tells him about being born of water and the Spirit (John 3), pointing back to Ezekiel 36. [Background] A Pharisee and 'a ruler of the Jews' who came to Jesus by night (John 3:1-2) and later helped bury Him (John 19:39).
- The disciples and the crowds: The audience again: the disciples, with the crowds who came and sat to hear. [Background] The Lord's Prayer is given to disciples: 'Pray, then, in this way' (6:9). Luke places it after a disciple asks, 'Lord, teach us to pray' (Luke 11:1).

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum: Jesus' home base. The white synagogue visitors see is later, built on an older basalt foundation.
- Magdala: A 1st-century synagogue, in use in Jesus' day, was uncovered here in 2009.
- Chorazin: Its basalt synagogue ruins date from a few centuries after Jesus.
- Arbel: Cliffs above the lake with the remains of a later synagogue.
- Mount of Beatitudes: The traditional site of the sermon.
- Tiberias: Herod Antipas' capital, founded around AD 20.
- Bethsaida: Home town of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44).
- Nazareth: Jesus' hometown, where He taught in the synagogue (Luke 4:16).

## Key terms
- Hypocrite: Greek hypokritēs: a stage actor, who played a part behind a mask. Jesus uses it for people whose religion is a performance.
- Righteousness (6:1): Here, acts of devotion: giving, prayer and fasting, the three pillars of Jewish piety. [Background]
- Giving to the poor (alms): Greek eleēmosynē, from eleos, mercy: the root of 'alms.' Linked to 'Blessed are the merciful' (5:7). [Background]
- Have their reward in full: Apechō was used on business receipts: 'paid in full.' The applause is all they will get. [Background]
- Chiasm: A mirrored pattern with a center. The video suggests the whole sermon and the Lord's Prayer may each be chiastic, and says this is debated.
- The Lord's Prayer: The model prayer of 6:9-13 (also Luke 11:2-4). The closing doxology, 'For Yours is the kingdom...,' is in brackets in the LSB because the earliest manuscripts lack it. [Background]
- Fasting: Going without food for a time to seek God. The Day of Atonement's 'humble your souls' (Leviticus 16:29) was kept by fasting; the Pharisee in Jesus' parable says, 'I fast twice a week' (Luke 18:12). [Background]
- New covenant: God's promise to write His law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31-34), the backdrop the video gives for the sermon.

## Hebrew and Greek words [Background; Strong's numbers follow the LSB's word tagging]
- μισθός misthos (G3408, Greek): Wages, pay, reward. The noun in 5:46 and 6:1, 2, 5, 16. (Matt 5:46; 6:1, 2, 5, 16)
- ἀποδίδωμι apodidōmi (G591, Greek): To give back, repay (LSB 'reward'). The Father's answer in 6:4, 6, 18. (Matt 6:4, 6, 18)
- ἀπέχω apechō (G568, Greek): To receive in full; a word used on receipts. Look up: BDAG, ἀπέχω. (Matt 6:2, 5, 16)
- ὑποκριτής hypokritēs (G5273, Greek): Actor, pretender: one who plays a part. (Matt 6:2, 5, 16)
- θεάομαι theaomai (G2300, Greek): To look at, behold, as a spectator (LSB 'noticed'). Related to theatron, 'theater.' (Matt 6:1)
- κρυπτός kryptos (G2927, Greek): Hidden, secret ('crypt'). 6:18 uses the related kryphaios (G2931a). (Matt 6:4, 6)
- ταμεῖον tameion (G5009, Greek): Inner room, storeroom. (Matt 6:6)
- βατταλογέω battalogeō (G945, Greek): To babble, use empty words (LSB 'use meaningless repetition'). Found only here in the New Testament. (Matt 6:7)
- ἁγιάζω hagiazō (G37, Greek): To make holy, treat as holy (LSB 'Hallowed'). (Matt 6:9)
- ἐπιούσιος epiousios (G1967, Greek): Daily: a rare word whose exact sense is debated ('for today,' 'for tomorrow,' or 'needed'). Look up: BDAG, ἐπιούσιος. (Matt 6:11)
- ὀφείλημα opheilēma (G3783, Greek): Debt; sin pictured as a debt owed to God. 6:14-15 switches to paraptōma, 'transgression.' (Matt 6:12)
- πειρασμός peirasmos (G3986, Greek): Testing, temptation: the same root as Jesus' testing in the wilderness (4:1). (Matt 6:13)
- ἀφανίζω aphanizō (G853, Greek): To make unseen, disfigure (LSB 'neglect their appearance'); a play on phainō, 'appear.' (Matt 6:16)
- νηστεύω nēsteuō (G3522, Greek): To fast. (Matt 6:16, 18)
- לֵב lev (H3820, Hebrew): Heart: the inner person, mind and will. 'On their heart I will write it.' (Jer 31:33; Ezek 36:26)
- בְּרִית berit (H1285, Hebrew): Covenant. (Jer 31:33)

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Three pillars of piety: Giving to the poor, prayer and fasting were the core acts of Jewish devotion. Jesus assumes His disciples will do all three: 'when you give,' 'when you pray,' 'when you fast.'
- Greek theater in Galilee: Theaters stood in the Decapolis cities and later in Sepphoris, near Nazareth, so 'hypocrite' was a familiar word. Actors wore masks to play their parts.
- Set times of prayer: Jews prayed at fixed times, often morning, afternoon and evening, wherever they were (compare Daniel 6:10; Acts 3:1). Being 'caught' on a street corner at prayer time could become a show.
- Fasting customs: The Pharisee in Jesus' parable fasts 'twice a week' (Luke 18:12); the Didache names Monday and Thursday as the 'hypocrites'' days. Fasters might skip washing and oiling their hair and wear sackcloth and ashes. Jesus says: look normal.
- The Lord's Prayer in the early church: The Didache, an early Christian manual (c. AD 100), gives the prayer in Matthew's form with a doxology and says: 'Thrice in the day thus pray.'

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- The Didache (c. AD 50-120): "Neither pray as the hypocrites; but as the Lord commanded in His Gospel, thus pray: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be Your name." Didache 8 (Roberts-Donaldson translation, public domain). It closes: 'Thrice in the day thus pray.'
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "And well has He called them hypocrites for the mask was of mercy, but the spirit of cruelty and inhumanity." Homilies on Matthew 19, on 6:2. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- Cyprian of Carthage (c. AD 252): "Our prayer is public and common; and when we pray, we pray not for one, but for the whole people, because we the whole people are one." On the Lord's Prayer, 8. Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Is the whole sermon a chiasm? Some scholars arrange Matthew 5-7 symmetrically with the Lord's Prayer at the center; others see a different structure (for example, 'the Law and the Prophets' at 5:17 and 7:12 framing the body). The video offers it as an invitation to study.
- Is the Lord's Prayer a chiasm? The video's center is 'on earth as it is in heaven.' Many read the prayer as three 'Your' petitions followed by three or four 'us' petitions. Either way, heaven's will on earth is a key line.
- Who are the hypocrites? The video stresses actors performing for applause. Others stress that Jesus' 'hypocrites' are also self-deceived: they 'say things and do not do them' (23:3). Both point to a gap between show and heart.
- 'Daily' bread Epiousios is almost unknown outside the Lord's Prayer: bread for today, for the coming day, or what is needed. Some early writers also read it of spiritual bread.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The captions say 'Matthew chapter 6 verses 1-8'; the passage read is 6:1-18.
- In English 'reward' repeats through 6:1-18, but Greek uses two words: the noun misthos (5:46; 6:1, 2, 5, 16) and the verb apodidōmi, 'repay' (6:4, 6, 18). The chain the video traces still holds.
- Hypokritēs did mean a stage actor. The touring troupes with trumpets and painted faces are an illustration rather than something the text says; Greek actors usually wore masks.
- 'Everything Jesus says in the Gospels is either a quotation from the Old Testament or an allusion to it' is a strong claim. Very much of it is, which is why the video's method works so well.
- The two chiasms (the whole sermon and the Lord's Prayer) are proposals; the video says so itself.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. The video's side study: list every word or phrase Jesus repeats in 6:1-18. What patterns do you see?
2. Why does the sermon need Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 behind it? What happens if we read it as 'just try harder'?
3. Which of the three (giving, prayer, fasting) do you find hardest to do 'in secret'? Why?
4. Pray the Lord's Prayer slowly. Which line stands out to you as the center this week?
5. The video says the commands reveal the Father. What does 6:1-18 show you about the Father's heart?
6. What is the lesson for you today?

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience: our heavenly Father extends His blessings to all, the just and the unjust, not to be seen but because He loves. So we perform our righteousness the same way, in secret, because our Father is in secret. Disciples must not act like actors blowing trumpets, but like the Father. The commands reveal His heart, His desires and His motives, and deeper understanding of the Father can lead to deeper intimacy with the Father. Now it's your turn: what is the lesson for you today?
- Study note (added): try one secret act this week from each of the three: give something no one will know about, pray once behind a shut door, and skip one meal to pray without telling anyone. Then ask the Father what He showed you.
